title: Why Use TSID?
description: Mint sortable, time-ordered unique identifiers from inside DuckDB SQL. [`tsid()`](#tsid) gives you the same property [UUIDv7](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562) and [ULID](https://github.com/ulid/spec) provide — IDs that sort chronologically by plain comparison — without leaving SQL or wiring an application-side library into your pipeline.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: DuckDB ships [`uuid()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/utility) — a UUIDv4 generator, random and unsortable. TSID fills the gap: a generator whose output sorts by creation time when compared as text. The same shape PostgreSQL users get from `gen_random_uuid()` plus `now()`, except the timestamp is embedded in the ID itself and recoverable.

bulletPoints.label: Surrogate primary keys that sort by insert time
bulletPoints.description: Use [`tsid()`](#tsid) as a column `DEFAULT`. `ORDER BY id` returns insert order — no separate `created_at` index needed for chronological scans.

bulletPoints.label: Audit-log and event identifiers
bulletPoints.description: B-tree friendly: new rows append at the high end of the index instead of scattering randomly the way [`uuid()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/utility) v4 does. Reduces page splits and improves cache locality on append-mostly tables.

bulletPoints.label: Time-range pagination cursors
bulletPoints.description: Because IDs are sortable strings, you can paginate by `WHERE id < :cursor ORDER BY id DESC` without joining a timestamp index — the [Twitter snowflake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake_ID) trick, in pure SQL.

bulletPoints.label: Embedded timestamp recovery
bulletPoints.description: [`tsid_to_timestamp`](#tsid_to_timestamp) decodes the leading bits back to a [`TIMESTAMP`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/data_types/timestamp). One column does the work of two.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: TSIDs are 128-bit identifiers rendered as 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters — the leading bits are a high-resolution timestamp, the trailing bits are random. The format is conceptually the same family as [UUIDv7](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562) and [ULID](https://github.com/ulid/spec); the rendering differs.

bulletPoints.label: Output type is VARCHAR, not BIGINT
bulletPoints.description: [`tsid()`](#tsid) returns a 32-character hex [`VARCHAR`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/data_types/text), the same width as a UUID hex string. Plain string comparison gives you time order — no special operator or cast required.

bulletPoints.label: Independent calls per row
bulletPoints.description: Each [`tsid()`](#tsid) call is independent — every row in `SELECT tsid() FROM range(N)` produces a fresh TSID. Within the millisecond resolution of the timestamp prefix, exact insertion order across rows of a parallel-evaluated query isn't guaranteed; if a strict total order matters, sort by an explicit `created_at` column rather than by the ID.

bulletPoints.label: Embedded timestamp
bulletPoints.description: [`tsid_to_timestamp`](#tsid_to_timestamp) decodes the leading bits to a `TIMESTAMP` with sub-millisecond precision. Same primitive UUIDv7-aware tools use to extract creation time from a v7 UUID.

bulletPoints.label: No external dependencies
bulletPoints.description: The extension generates IDs in-process — no network call, no clock-server coordination. Safe to use as a column `DEFAULT` in [`CREATE TABLE`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/statements/create_table) without latency surprises.

sections.title: TSID vs UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 vs ULID
sections.description: All four occupy the same niche — opaque, unique, application-mintable IDs. The differences are about ordering, rendering, and standardization.

bulletPoints.label: vs UUIDv4 (DuckDB built-in [`uuid()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/utility))
bulletPoints.description: UUIDv4 is random — great for collision avoidance, terrible for B-tree locality and unusable for time-ordered pagination. TSID wins anywhere insert order, recent-first scans, or index-append behavior matters.

bulletPoints.label: vs UUIDv7 ([RFC 9562](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562))
bulletPoints.description: UUIDv7 is the IETF-standardized time-sortable UUID. Functionally TSID and UUIDv7 cover the same ground; UUIDv7 wins on portability (every modern UUID library understands it), TSID wins because DuckDB ships v4 only and TSID gives you the v7-shaped behavior without bringing your own generator.

bulletPoints.label: vs ULID ([ulid/spec](https://github.com/ulid/spec))
bulletPoints.description: ULID is the same idea — millisecond-precision time prefix plus random tail — rendered in 26-character Crockford base32. TSID's hex rendering is two characters wider but lines up cleanly with how DuckDB users already format UUIDs, and avoids Crockford-base32 ambiguity edge cases.

sections.title: Caveats
sections.description: Things to know before reaching for TSID over a built-in UUID.

bulletPoints.label: TSIDs leak creation time
bulletPoints.description: The timestamp is recoverable by anyone holding the ID — that's the feature, but it's also a privacy and competitive-intelligence concern. Don't use TSIDs as public-facing identifiers for resources where the creation moment is sensitive (signup time, order placement, account creation). [`uuid()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/utility) v4 stays the right choice for opaque external IDs.

bulletPoints.label: Not an IETF or de-facto standard
bulletPoints.description: Unlike [UUIDv7](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9562) (RFC 9562) or [ULID](https://github.com/ulid/spec) (widely adopted spec), the TSID rendering is library-specific. The conceptual primitive — time prefix + random tail — is portable; the exact 32-hex layout produced here may not parse with TSID libraries from other ecosystems such as [`f4b6a3/tsid-creator`](https://github.com/f4b6a3/tsid-creator). Stay self-contained, or pin the format you serialize to disk.

bulletPoints.label: VARCHAR storage, not BINARY
bulletPoints.description: Each TSID occupies 32 bytes as text — twice the 16 bytes a binary UUID column needs in some engines. DuckDB's dictionary encoding compresses this well in practice, but plan for it on multi-billion-row tables where every byte counts.

bulletPoints.label: Experimental status
bulletPoints.description: The upstream README marks the extension experimental. The exposed surface is small ([`tsid`](#tsid), [`tsid_to_timestamp`](#tsid_to_timestamp)), so churn risk is low — but pin a known-good version in production schemas that depend on the on-disk hex layout.

useCases.title: Primary keys for append-mostly tables
useCases.description: Use [`tsid()`](#tsid) as `DEFAULT` on the primary-key column of an event log, audit table, or message store. New rows append at the index head, `ORDER BY id` is `ORDER BY created_at`, and you can drop a redundant timestamp column.

useCases.title: Recent-first pagination without timestamp join
useCases.description: Paginate by `WHERE id < :cursor ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT N` — no separate `created_at` index, no `OFFSET` cost on large tables. The Twitter-snowflake / cursor-pagination pattern, available in plain DuckDB.

useCases.title: Drop a `created_at` column
useCases.description: When the only thing a `created_at` column does is record insertion time, replace it with a TSID primary key and recover the timestamp via [`tsid_to_timestamp`](#tsid_to_timestamp) when you need it. One column instead of two.

useCases.title: Replacement for `uuid()` where ordering matters
useCases.description: Anywhere you'd reach for [`uuid()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/utility) but actually wanted UUIDv7-style ordering, [`tsid()`](#tsid) is the in-DuckDB equivalent. No application-side generator, no client library.
